cards.title: Phase difference between the e-ray and the o-ray
cards.legend: A plate of thickness d is cut with its optic axis parallel to the faces; light falls normally. The o-ray (vibration perpendicular to the optic axis) and the e-ray (vibration along it) travel the same way, drawn apart here for clarity, with indices μ_o and μ_e. Bars below show the optical paths μ_o d and μ_e d drawn to scale for calcite (μ_o = 1.658, μ_e = 1.486, μ_o > μ_e). Δ is the optical path difference and δ the phase difference on leaving the plate.

phases.name: Optical paths

phases.name: Phase difference
phases.why: convert path to phase with 2π per wavelength

steps.note: Start with the o-ray. Optical path in the crystal is the refractive index times the thickness, so the o-ray has optical path \(\mu_o d\) in a plate of thickness \(d\).

ask.q: Which index sets the optical path of the o-ray in the plate?
ask.why: Optical path is the index of the ray's own medium times the geometric thickness, here \(\mu_o d\).

steps.note: The e-ray crosses the same thickness \(d\) but with index \(\mu_e\), so its optical path is \(\mu_e d\).

The optical path difference between the two waves is the difference of the two optical paths. Calcite has \(\mu_o > \mu_e\) so \(\Delta\) is positive (the book states it as \(e\)- minus \(o\) in magnitude).

figure.caption: Path difference Δ = difference of the bars

steps.note: Replace \(L_o\) and \(L_e\) by the two optical paths found above.
Both terms contain the same thickness \(d\), so take it out as a common factor (Eq. 20.35).

ask.q: In calcite (\(\mu_o > \mu_e\)), what sign does \(\Delta = (\mu_o-\mu_e)d\) have?
ask.why: A negative uniaxial crystal has \(\mu_o>\mu_e\), so \(\mu_o-\mu_e>0\) and \(\Delta>0\).

steps.note: A path difference of one wavelength \(\lambda\) is a phase difference of \(2\pi\). So the phase difference is the same fraction of \(2\pi\) as the path difference is of \(\lambda\).

ask.q: A path difference of exactly one wavelength corresponds to a phase difference of
ask.why: One full wave is one full cycle of phase, \(2\pi\).

steps.note: Put \(\Delta = (\mu_o-\mu_e)d\) into the phase relation (Eq. 20.36). The two waves left the front face in phase and now have this constant phase difference.

ask.q: Why can the o- and e-rays not produce interference fringes even though \(\delta\) is constant?
options: Their planes of polarisation are perpendicular
ask.why: Perpendicular vibrations do not interfere; they combine into an elliptically polarised wave (see §20.18).

The bars are to scale for calcite (μ_o = 1.658, μ_e = 1.486) and d as drawn, so Δ equals one quarter of the wavelength λ shown at the bottom. δ is the phase difference.

phases.why: set Δ = (μ_o − μ_e)d equal to λ/4 and solve for d

phases.name: Phase
phases.why: convert the λ/4 path to a 90° phase difference

steps.note: A quarter-wave plate is cut so that the path difference \(\Delta = (\mu_o-\mu_e)d\) of §20.17 equals a quarter of a wavelength (Eq. 20.48).

ask.q: What path difference must a quarter-wave plate introduce?
ask.why: By definition it is a quarter of a wavelength, a phase difference of \(90^\circ\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(\mu_o-\mu_e\) to isolate the thickness (Eq. 20.49).

ask.why: \(d\) is multiplied by \(\mu_o-\mu_e\), so divide by it.

steps.note: The phase difference follows from the path difference in the usual way: \(2\pi\) of phase per wavelength of path (§20.17).

The wavelength \(\lambda\) cancels, leaving \(\delta = \pi/2 = 90^\circ\). A quarter-wave plate therefore turns plane-polarised light into elliptically or circularly polarised light, depending on the angle between the incident vibration and the optic axis.

steps.note: For a half-wave plate the path difference \(\Delta = (\mu_o-\mu_e)d\) of §20.17 must equal half a wavelength (Eq. 20.50).

ask.q: What path difference must a half-wave plate introduce?
ask.why: By definition, half a wavelength, which is a phase difference of \(180^\circ\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(\mu_o-\mu_e\) (Eq. 20.51). This is twice the thickness of the quarter-wave plate made of the same crystal.
Use the relation between phase and path difference (§20.17).
The wavelength cancels, so \(\delta = \pi = 180^\circ\). The two waves leave in opposite phase.
